passage:
Team lead's note, for my own records
Today several of us went to the funeral of Arvind's father. Madhuri (25), who joined the team in March, was calm on the drive there. When the prayers began, she started to shake, then sobbed, much harder than anyone else there.
In the car afterwards she said, "My mother died when I was seven. I haven't cried about her in years. I thought I was done." She seemed surprised at herself.
I didn't try to explain it away. I told her it made sense and offered her tomorrow off; she said yes. I also gave her the number of our staff counselling line, in case the feelings keep coming.
Check in with her on Monday.
— Vandana

qa.q: Whose funeral did the team attend?
qa.a: The funeral of Arvind's father.

qa.q: Why was Madhuri surprised at herself in the car?
qa.a: Madhuri believed the grief for her mother was long finished, so being flooded by it at someone else's funeral felt unexpected.

qa.q: What did Vandana choose to do after the funeral, and why did it fit?
qa.a: Vandana accepted the tears as making sense and offered a day off and the counselling number, giving the returning grief room instead of pushing it away.

qa.q: How might Madhuri's colleagues have seen her sobbing at the funeral?
qa.a: They may have been puzzled at first, since she was calmer on the drive and barely knew the family, until they understood her own loss.

grounding: A team lead's note records a young woman flooded by grief for her mother, who died when she was seven, at a colleague's father's funeral.

passage:
Sunday, late
Held Kunal today for the first time. Didi's son, three days old, so light he felt like a folded towel.
And out of nowhere I was crying. Not happy crying. The kind where you can't breathe properly.
I think it's about Chhotu. My baby brother, who died when I was five. I haven't thought about him in years. I didn't think I remembered him at all. But the weight of Kunal in my arms, and that milky smell, and suddenly I was five again in Nani's courtyard with everyone whispering.
Didi took Kunal back and just held my hand.
I don't know what to do with this yet. Writing it down helps a little.
— Bhavna

qa.q: How old was Kunal when Bhavna held him?
qa.a: Three days old.

qa.q: Why did holding Kunal bring Chhotu back so suddenly?
qa.a: The weight and milky smell of a newborn matched an early loss Bhavna had packed away, so the old sadness and grieving for Chhotu came back all at once.

qa.q: What could help Bhavna with the grief that has resurfaced?
qa.a: Going on writing and talking to Didi or another trusted person about Chhotu; if the sadness keeps going or feels too heavy, a counsellor could help.

qa.q: What might Didi have understood when she took Kunal back and held Bhavna's hand?
qa.a: Didi probably sensed the tears were about more than the baby, and chose quiet comfort over questions.

grounding: Holding a newborn nephew floods a young adult with grief for a baby brother lost in early childhood and thought forgotten.

passage: In the courtyard of his sister's house in Malegaon, Asif, twenty-five, was handed his newborn nephew for the first time. The baby's fingers curled around his thumb. Everyone was laughing, taking photos. And suddenly Asif couldn't breathe properly. A wave came up from nowhere: his own Ammi, gone when he was six, the smell of her dupatta, a lullaby he hadn't thought of in twenty years. Tears ran down his face before he could stop them. He hadn't cried for her since he was a boy. He'd thought all that was long finished. His friend Karthik, standing by the gate, stepped in, took the baby gently, and walked Asif to the back steps. "Sit," Karthik said, and sat beside him, saying nothing. The lullaby kept going round in Asif's head, and he let it.

qa.q: How old was Asif when his Ammi died?
qa.a: He was six.

qa.q: Why was Asif so surprised by his tears while holding the baby?
qa.a: He believed his grief for his Ammi was long finished, yet holding a newborn brought the old loss flooding back without warning.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that helped in that moment?
qa.a: Karthik quietly took the baby, walked Asif to the back steps, and sat beside him without asking questions.

qa.q: How might Asif's sister feel seeing him cry while holding her baby?
qa.a: She might be surprised, and perhaps moved, realising the moment reminded him of the mother they lost.

grounding: A young man holding his newborn nephew is flooded by grief for his mother, a loss he thought he had long put behind him.

passage: Tariq, twenty-four, went to the funeral of his colleague's father in Leeds mostly out of politeness. He had barely met the man. He stood at the back of the chapel with his friend Liam. Then the family played an old piano piece, and a grandson, maybe eight, stood at the front holding his mother's hand, trying hard not to cry. Tariq's chest tightened. He was eight again, at his own grandfather's burial in Lahore, the smell of rain and rosewater, being told to be a brave boy. He had never cried for his grandfather. He thought he'd forgotten most of it. Now his eyes stung so badly he had to step outside. Liam followed and stood with him by the wall. "I don't even know why," Tariq said. "Maybe you do," Liam said quietly.

qa.q: Where was Tariq's grandfather buried?
qa.a: In Lahore.

qa.q: Why did the grandson at the front affect Tariq so strongly?
qa.a: Seeing a boy his own age then brought back his grandfather's burial, and Tariq was overwhelmed by grief he had never let out.

qa.q: What could Tariq do with this feeling now that it has returned?
qa.a: He could let himself talk about his grandfather with Liam or someone close, instead of pushing the grief away again.

qa.q: How might Liam see Tariq's reaction at the funeral of a man Tariq barely knew?
qa.a: Liam seems to understand that the tears are about something older, and stays close without making Tariq explain.

grounding: At a funeral, a young man is overwhelmed by grief for his grandfather, a childhood loss he thought he had forgotten.

passage: In the maternity ward of the Aurangabad hospital, Minakshi handed her newborn daughter to her brother. "Hold her properly, Samir." Samir cradled the tiny girl. She yawned. And something cracked open in his chest. Suddenly he was six again, standing by a cot in his grandmother's house, and the baby in it was his little brother, Aarif, who only lived three weeks. He hadn't thought of Aarif in years. He'd thought it was gone, a fact from long ago, like an old address. Now his eyes were streaming. "Samir?" Minakshi said. "Bhai, what's wrong?" "Aarif," he managed. Minakshi went quiet. She had been too little to remember. A nurse, passing, pulled the curtain gently around them and left a box of tissues on the chair.

qa.q: How long did Aarif live?
qa.a: Only three weeks.

qa.q: Why did holding the baby flood Samir with grief?
qa.a: Holding a newborn echoed the moment by his baby brother's cot, bringing back a grief he thought had faded, so he was suddenly overwhelmed.

qa.q: What could help Samir after this moment?
qa.a: Talking about Aarif with Minakshi or another trusted person, and seeking a counsellor if the grief keeps returning strongly.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Samir says "Aarif"?
qa.a: Minakshi may feel shocked and sad, as she was too little to remember, and touched to see how much her brother still carried.

grounding: Shows an adult holding a new baby and being flooded with grief for an early loss he thought was long forgotten.

passage:
Dear Rafiq,

I'm writing because I can't make sense of today and you're the only one who won't rush me.

I went to Shalini's father's funeral. I barely knew him. I went for her. And during the prayers, when her little brother came forward to lay the flowers, I started crying so hard I had to leave the hall.

It wasn't about Shalini's father. It was Ma. I was eight when she died. I was the one who stood there with the flowers. I thought that was long done, packed away. I haven't cried about her in fifteen years.

I sat in the car park for an hour. I feel embarrassed and also like something's been opened that I can't close.

Can we talk this weekend?

Binita

qa.q: How old was Binita when Ma died?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: Why did Binita cry so hard at the funeral?
qa.a: Seeing a child lay flowers mirrored Binita's own loss at eight, bringing back grief that felt packed away, so Binita was flooded and overwhelmed.

qa.q: What makes reaching out to Rafiq a good step?
qa.a: Talking with a trusted, patient person lets the old grief be heard instead of packed away again; if it stays heavy, a counsellor could help too.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel if she learned why Binita left the hall?
qa.a: Shalini might feel moved and sad for Binita, and understand the grief was about more than her own father.

grounding: Shows an adult at a funeral flooded by grief tied to an early loss that seemed long forgotten.

passage: Maria, you asked why I disappeared from the naming ceremony. Here's what happened to me, Harsha. Everything was fine. Priya's baby was sleeping, people were eating sweets. Then her grandmother picked up the baby and began to sing a lullaby, a Kannada one, very old. And I just broke. I was seven again, and my mother was singing that exact song to me, a month before she died. I hadn't heard it in eighteen years. I didn't even know I remembered it. I went to the bathroom and cried until my face hurt. It wasn't sadness like a thought; it was like a wave coming up from the floor. I thought I had finished grieving her when I was a kid. Apparently not. Some part of me had just been keeping it very quietly.

qa.q: How old was Harsha when the mother died?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: Why did the lullaby affect Harsha so strongly?
qa.a: It was the song Harsha's mother sang just before she died, so hearing it brought back buried grief as an overwhelming wave.

qa.q: What could Harsha do now that the grief has surfaced?
qa.a: Harsha could talk to a trusted friend like Maria about the mother, and see a counsellor if the grief stays heavy.

qa.q: How might Priya's grandmother feel if she knew the lullaby's effect?
qa.a: She might feel sorry and tender, never having meant her song to bring back such pain.

grounding: Shows an adult at a baby's naming ceremony flooded by grief tied to an early loss thought long forgotten.

passage:
Monday. Rafiq, twenty-five, held his sister Jahnavi's newborn for the first time at the hospital in Hyderabad. The baby's tiny hand closed around his finger. Suddenly, his eyes filled with tears. He passed the baby back and left the room.

Tuesday. He couldn't stop thinking about his younger brother, who had died as a baby when Rafiq was five. He hadn't thought about it in years.

Friday. Jahnavi found him on her balcony, quiet. "Is it about our little brother?" she asked. Rafiq nodded. He cried then, properly. She sat with him. "I think about him too," she said. Later that week, Rafiq called his mother and asked her to tell him about the baby brother he barely remembered.

qa.q: How old was Rafiq when his younger brother died?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq cry when holding the newborn?
qa.a: Holding a baby brought back grief for his brother, a feeling he thought was long forgotten.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do later that week, and why might it help?
qa.a: He called his mother to hear about his brother, letting the old grief be spoken instead of buried.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel sitting with Rafiq?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably feels sad and tender, sharing the same loss.

grounding: An adult holding a newborn is flooded by grief tied to a brother's early death he thought was forgotten.

passage:
Rukmini, you asked why I cried so much at your grandmother's funeral last year. Let your Shalini masi tell you.

When I was twenty-four, I went to a colleague's father's funeral. I barely knew the man. But as soon as I saw the family sitting on the floor, I started crying so hard I had to go outside.

I didn't understand at first. Then I remembered: when I was six, my own father died. I'd been sent to a neighbour's house during his funeral. I had never cried for him, not really. I'd thought it was forgotten.

It wasn't. It had been waiting all those years. That day I finally cried for Papa.

qa.q: What happened to Shalini's father when she was six?
qa.a: Her father died.

qa.q: Why did young Shalini cry so hard at a stranger's funeral?
qa.a: Seeing the family brought back grief for her father that she had never let out, a feeling she thought was forgotten.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Shalini grieve for her father?
qa.a: The colleague's father's funeral stirred the buried feeling, and that day she finally cried for Papa.

qa.q: How might Shalini's colleague have seen her crying?
qa.a: The colleague might have felt surprised but touched, not knowing it was about Shalini's own father.

grounding: An elder recalls being flooded with grief at a funeral, tied to her father's death she thought was forgotten.

passage:
Mohit had only an hour at his cousin Anirban's wedding before his train back to Pune. The hall was noisy, the music loud. Then the priest invited the families to bless the couple. Anirban's mother stepped forward alone, holding a framed photo of his late father.

Mohit's throat closed. He had to step outside into the heat.

He thought of his own mother, who had died when he was eight. He hadn't cried about her in years. He'd thought he'd moved on.

Anirban found him by the gate. "You okay?"

"It's Ma," Mohit said, surprised by his own words.

Anirban put an arm round him. They stood together until the train was nearly due.

qa.q: What was Anirban's mother holding?
qa.a: A framed photo of his late father.

qa.q: Why did Mohit have to step outside?
qa.a: Seeing the photo brought a flood of grief for his own mother, a feeling he thought he'd moved past.

qa.q: What small step helped Mohit in that moment?
qa.a: Saying "It's Ma" out loud to Anirban, who stayed with him.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel finding Mohit at the gate?
qa.a: Anirban probably felt concerned and understanding, since he also lost a parent.

grounding: At a wedding, an adult is flooded by grief tied to his mother's death he thought was long forgotten.

passage: In the hospital room in Pune, Rukmini placed her newborn daughter in her sister Aditi's arms. The baby's tiny fist closed around Aditi's finger. And suddenly Aditi was crying, not gently, but in deep, shaking waves. Rukmini stared. "Didi? What's wrong?" Aditi couldn't answer. She hadn't cried about their mother in twenty years. She had been six when Amma died, and she always said she barely remembered her. But the baby's smell and soft weight brought back an old lullaby, a hand stroking her hair. "I miss Amma," she managed finally. "I didn't know I still did." Rukmini put an arm around her, and they sat together, the baby asleep between them.

qa.q: How old was Aditi when Amma died?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why did Aditi suddenly cry while holding the baby?
qa.a: The baby's smell and weight brought back her mother's lullaby, flooding her with grief she thought was long forgotten.

qa.q: What might help Aditi after this?
qa.a: Letting herself grieve, talking with Rukmini about Amma, and speaking to a counsellor if the grief stays overwhelming.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel seeing her sister cry?
qa.a: Surprised and worried at first, then tender, sharing the loss as she puts an arm around her.

grounding: An adult holding a newborn is flooded by grief for a mother lost in childhood that she thought was forgotten.

passage:
"Kamal, you're shaking. Sit down."
"I'm fine. I barely knew Mr Rao."
"You've been crying since the prayers."
"It's stupid. It's the incense. And the white sheet. I don't know."
Dilnaz handed him water. "When did you last go to a funeral?"
He was silent for a long time. "Abbu's. I was ten."
"Did you cry then?"
"No. Everyone said I was brave."
"Maybe it's that grief, then. Waiting."
"Fifteen years, Dilnaz. I thought it was done."
"Maybe it just needed a door."
He covered his face. She sat beside him and didn't say anything else.

qa.q: How old was Kamal at Abbu's funeral?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: Why is Kamal crying at the funeral of someone he barely knew?
qa.a: The incense and the white sheet brought back unshed grief for his father, held in since everyone called him brave at ten.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do that helped?
qa.a: She sat him down, gave him water, gently asked about his last funeral, and then simply stayed beside him without more words.

qa.q: What is it like for Dilnaz to watch Kamal break down?
qa.a: She is concerned and gentle, understanding before he does that an old grief is surfacing.

grounding: An adult at a funeral is flooded by grief for a father lost in childhood, long thought to be over.

passage: Last spring my best friend Ujjwal asked me to hold his son at the naming ceremony. I'm Uday, and I'm not a crier. But as the priest said the baby's name and the little one yawned against my chest, something cracked open. I remembered my own father lifting me onto his shoulders at a fair. He died when I was four. For twenty years I had told everyone I didn't remember him. Apparently some part of me did. I handed the baby back and went and stood in the corridor, crying into my sleeve. Ujjwal found me and just stood there with me. Later I started writing down what I remembered about my father. It was more than I thought.

qa.q: What did Uday remember the father doing?
qa.a: Lifting Uday onto his shoulders at a fair.

qa.q: What did Uday feel while holding the baby?
qa.a: Something cracked open: grief for the father who died when Uday was four, long thought forgotten, suddenly flooded back.

qa.q: What did Uday do with the feeling afterwards?
qa.a: Began writing down memories of the father, giving the old grief a place instead of pushing it away.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt finding Uday in the corridor?
qa.a: Concerned and caring, choosing simply to stand there as quiet support.

grounding: An adult holding a friend's baby is flooded by grief for a father lost in early childhood that had seemed forgotten.

passage:
Ward note, maternity wing, Pongal week.
Anjali's brother, Karthik, visited this afternoon with sugarcane stalks for the new mother. When I placed the baby girl in his arms, he smiled for a moment, then his face crumpled. He handed her back quickly and stood at the window, shoulders shaking.
Afterwards he told me, embarrassed, that their mother died when he was four, a week after a Pongal just like this one. "I haven't thought about her properly in twenty years. I thought I was over it." Anjali held his hand and said she had felt the same during labour.
I sat with them for a while, told Karthik that feelings like this often come back at births, and gave him the hospital counsellor's number in case the grief keeps returning.

qa.q: What did Karthik bring when he visited the maternity wing?
qa.a: Sugarcane stalks for the new mother.

qa.q: Why was Karthik embarrassed after he cried?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and caught off guard, because he believed he was over his mother's death, and holding the baby flooded him with grief he thought was long gone.

qa.q: How could Karthik look after himself in the coming weeks?
qa.a: He could let himself talk about their mother with Anjali, and use the counsellor's number if the grief keeps returning or feels too heavy.

qa.q: How is Anjali affected by seeing Karthik cry?
qa.a: She understands him because she felt the same during labour, and holding his hand shows the shared loss drawing them closer.

grounding: A young adult holding a newborn is suddenly flooded with grief for a mother lost in early childhood.
